name: Priya Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for taking the time, Priya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an operator on the bottling line at a soft drinks plant, the one that does the supermarket own-brand lemonade and cola. I run the filler and the capper, so I set the fill heights, change the cap feed when we switch flavours, and keep an eye on the reject counter. A changeover from cola to lemonade takes forty minutes of cleaning and I can do it in thirty-two, which I'm a bit smug about.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what's tough?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the changeovers, because that's where you can tell who knows the line. The tough part is twelve-hour shifts in summer when the orders spike. By the fourth one my feet are done and I'm short with everyone.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Kofi, he's a sous-chef at a hotel, so our hours never match. We rent a one-bed above a bakery. We've got maybe two and a half months saved, it was more before the car needed a gearbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read the card as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of noise for not much, but the bits that work are handy. At work I'd say the new scheduling software got the summer rota right for once. Online I'd probably not say anything, I just scroll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it's good for me. Own-brand drinks sell more when money's tight, so the bottling plant stays busy. My only worry is building the savings back up after the gearbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and try to get back to four months saved by next summer, by working the overtime in July and August. I'd use the AI on my phone now and then to plan meals around Kofi's shifts, which sounds silly but it saves money. And I'd go for the team leader job if it came up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Bit impatient to get the savings back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the gearbox affect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It cost one thousand four hundred, nearly half our savings. We need the car because the plant's on the bypass and the first bus is after my shift starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being team leader mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More money, maybe ten percent, and I'd get to set the changeover standard for everyone. I already do it, so I might as well be paid for it.

say: I'd say it was a lot of **noise** for not much.
I'd admit the **scheduling software** got the rota right.
think: I think the plant is **busy** because own-brand drinks sell when money's tight.
My real worry is rebuilding **savings** after the gearbox.
do: Work **summer overtime** to get back to four months saved.
Use the **AI app** now and then to plan cheaper meals.
Apply for **team leader** if it comes up.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit impatient to rebuild **savings**.
S0.quote: Own-brand drinks sell more when money's tight, so the bottling plant stays busy.
fieldNote: Priya sees her plant as **recession-proof** because of own-brand demand.
A **gearbox** bill halved savings, which is her main pressure.
She wants the **team leader** title for work she already does.

steps.text: Work July and August overtime to reach four months saved
Use the AI app to plan cheaper meals around Kofi's shifts
Keep running the filler and apply for team leader

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read the card as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots more slowly. That's realistic, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office will feel it and the line will feel it later. With friends I'd say it's sensible to learn a bit now. I wouldn't make a fuss online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the planning and ordering at our plant is probably going to software, and then the robots will come for the palletising first, then the changeovers. I've got a few years. But my thirty-two-minute changeover is exactly the kind of skill a machine will copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the plant down the road does, they always buy new kit first. Once a couple of people I know have done it, I'd do the quality technician course, it's a year part-time. I'd keep saving and not take on any new debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why quality technician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to test the drinks and sign off the batch, and that's a responsible job. Even if AI does the testing, someone gets the blame when it's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Kofi say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say do it, and then ask who's cooking on my study nights. We'd work it out.

say: I'd say the **office** feels it first and the line later.
I'd tell friends it's sensible to **learn a bit** now.
think: I think robots take the **palletising** first, then the changeovers.
My **changeover skill** is what a machine will copy.
do: Watch what the **plant down the road** buys first.
Do the **quality technician** course part-time after others try it.
S1.quote: My thirty-two-minute changeover is exactly the kind of skill a machine will copy.
fieldNote: Priya is proud of her **changeover** speed and sees it as exposed.
Her steady style shows: she'll **follow** others onto the course.
She values **responsibility** as something that may outlast automation.

steps.text: Watch how the neighbouring plant automates before choosing a course
Do the one-year part-time quality technician course
Keep saving and take on no new debt

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read the card as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028. That's really fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, and it should be practical, not just speeches. At work I'd say let's not panic and let's get training. Online I'd share anything useful, like grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the quality job I was eyeing is thinking work, so AGI takes it in 2028. The line itself lasts until robots come in 2031. So I'd be standing at a filler for three years knowing the clock's running, with no clear next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the savings to six months fast, cut the car insurance by shopping around, stop the weekend trips. I'd look at jobs where you deal with people face to face, maybe the hotel where Kofi works, front of house. I'd keep going on the line while I looked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd keep busy so I don't think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said front of house. Doesn't AGI touch that too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the booking side, yes. But people at a hotel want a person at the desk, I think. I'm guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Kofi's job? Is a kitchen safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that scares me. Robots in kitchens by 2031, maybe. If my job and my partner Kofi's kitchen job both go in the same few years, we'd have nothing coming in.

say: I'd ask government for a **practical plan**, not speeches.
I'd tell people at work to get **training** and not panic.
think: I think AGI takes the **quality job** I wanted in 2028.
I'd spend **three years** at the filler knowing the clock is running.
do: Reach **six months** saved by cutting insurance and weekend trips.
Look at **front of house** work at Kofi's hotel.
Keep working the **line** while I look.
feel: **Anxious**, keeping busy so I don't think about it.
S2.quote: If my job and my partner Kofi's kitchen job both go in the same few years, we'd have nothing coming in.
fieldNote: Priya realises her planned move is **thinking work** that goes first.
The real fear is **both incomes** going at once.
She hedges honestly: front of house is a **guess**.

steps.text: Shop around to cut the car insurance
Build savings to six months within the year
Ask about front of house jobs at Kofi's hotel
Keep running the filler while looking for work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read the card as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, there's a bit more room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if people start now. At work I'd push the managers to say what their plan is. Online I'd keep quiet as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots by 2034 means I'd be on the line until I'm about thirty-five. That's long enough to save and move. But the thinking parts of the job, the scheduling and the quality sign-off, go in 2031, so the team leader job I want is shaky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see what others do, then pick something hands-on with people, maybe a trade like electrician. I'd save hard for the first two years. Kofi and I would hold off on getting married until we know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan forming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why put the wedding off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wedding is ten thousand we don't have, and if the jobs are going, that money is our cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is an electrician hands-on enough to last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old houses, odd wiring, crawling under floors. I think robots will be slow at that. I'd ask an electrician first before I signed up.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough time if people start now.
I'd push the plant managers to tell us their **plan** for the line.
think: I think I'd be on the line until about **thirty-five**.
The **team leader** job is shaky, because scheduling goes in 2031.
do: **Wait** a year to see what others do.
Hold off on the **wedding** and save.
S3.quote: A wedding is ten thousand we don't have, and if the jobs are going, that money is our cushion.
fieldNote: Priya would delay the **wedding** to protect savings.
She picks an **electrician** trade for old, awkward houses.
Her steady style means a **year of watching** first.

steps.text: Watch for a year how others at the plant move
Ask an electrician, then start a part-time apprenticeship
Postpone the wedding with Kofi and keep the money saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read the card as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable-ish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and I'd mean it. At work I'd say we should be asking the company for training now while it's cheap for them. I'd probably post about it once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay. I'd be thirty-nine by 2039, I could do team leader for a few years and then move to a trade. The worry is just that I'll get comfy and forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for team leader now and take the money. Around year four I'd start the electrician course. We'd get married and maybe think about a baby around thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you forget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Life. Overtime, Kofi's shifts, a holiday. Ten years goes like two if you're busy, so I'd put a reminder in my phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the plant would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office ladies who do the orders. They get hit in 2036, and they're in their fifties now, so they'd be early sixties. Maybe they'd just retire.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty of time, and I'd mean it.
I'd ask the company for **training now** while it's still cheap for them.
think: I think I'd be **okay**, doing team leader then a trade.
My worry is getting **comfy** and forgetting.
do: Start the **electrician course** around year four.
Go ahead with the **wedding** and maybe a baby.
S4.quote: Ten years goes like two if you're busy, so I'd put a reminder in my phone.
fieldNote: Priya trusts the long warning but fears her own **complacency**.
Her plan is a **ladder**: team leader, then a trade.
Family plans go **ahead** only in this picture.

steps.text: Apply for team leader on the bottling line
Start an electrician course around year four
Go ahead with the wedding and plan a baby around thirty

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because both our jobs could go close together and we'd have no time to switch. What would help is clear information about which trades will last, and money to live on while we retrain. Not a speech, a plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about couples. Everyone asks about one job. When you're two people renting, it's the two jobs together that decide if you're okay.

headlineQuote: When you're two people renting, it's the two jobs together that decide if you're okay.
portrait: Priya is a **27-year-old** bottling line operator at a soft drinks plant.
She rents above a bakery with Kofi, a **sous-chef**, and is rebuilding savings after a **gearbox** bill.
She's practical and **steady**, waiting to see what others try before moving.
Her biggest fear is **both incomes** going at once in the fast AGI picture.
With ten years' warning she'd climb to **team leader** and then retrain as an electrician.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job and Kofi's could go **together**.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information on **lasting trades** and **living money** while retraining.
